title: Chicago breakfast dances and 'Deep Forest' for Earl Hines
summary: He describes breakfast dances in Chicago, his embarrassing playing of Hines's theme, and telling Hines about it years later in Nice.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: But we got in Chicago and I went around every morning to the breakfast dance. You see, they had a breakfast dance. This is a thing they had every morning. They used to have those here. They called it a breakfast dance, it's just where they had a special show...say at four o'clock, the place closed at four or five o'clock. They'd have music and a dance

and all of the people...I guess it was one way that each club would have of increasing its business and, you know, people who wouldn't have an opportunity to go could go. So, they had breakfast dances every morning at one of the different clubs. And I never will forget, on Sunday night it was at the Club De-Lisa that would have...that's where Albert Ammons was playing, you know. And they had a big show and all that, and they'd have this big breakfast dance and hundreds of people, you know, come and try to get in, you know, and people from other clubs and people from the Panama. This is where King Cole used to play. And people from the DeLuxe. And Jimmie Noone's band, and Teddy Wilson's band, and musicians that played out on the north side, you know what I mean, the white spots. And downtown. They would all come to these various breakfast dances.

And I never will forget one morning, they had a breakfast dance at 49th and South Parkway.// Earl Hines came in with a party and I jumped up from my table and ran over to the piano and started playing "Deep Forest." That's his theme song. And the people thought I was crazy, you know. "Man, don't you see Earl Hines"? and "What are you trying to play his song...," you know. I only wanted to let Earl Hines know that I loved him so, that I knew his song. But the guys made it look like that I was crazy. So I had to sneak out the back door, you know what I mean. They gave me hell and I never mentioned that to Earl, that I was the guy that did that. But years later, in 1974...'76, we played the festival in Nice. He and

I were featured together. And that's when I told him that I was the guy that did that, and he laughed like hell. He said, "I wondered what that foolishness." He said, "Well where did you go?" I said, "Well, I went home and got under the cover, I was so embarassed."
